judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 145. The act makes it easy to get out of a subscription that renews itself. A seller that signed a customer up online has to offer a one-step online cancellation link. One-step means the customer needs no further steps after clicking. The seller can send that link by email or put it where the customer manages the account. The rule also covers trial offers that turn into paid subscriptions. Breaking it is a deceptive trade practice, and the attorney general can write rules. The Colorado House passed it 41-22 and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 79. The act regulates the kiosks that sell cryptocurrency for cash. A new customer can spend at most $2,000 a day at a kiosk, and an existing customer $10,500. The kiosk has to show set warnings on screen, including its refund policy. The customer has to confirm they saw them. A first-time customer who is defrauded gets a full refund if police confirm the fraud within the time the act allows. The Colorado House passed it 48-14 and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 126. Big company mergers have to be reported to federal antitrust regulators. The act makes the same filing go to the Colorado attorney general. That applies when the company is based here, or sells enough here. On request, the company has to hand over the supporting material within seven days. The attorney general cannot charge a fee for the filing, and can share material with other states. The Colorado Senate passed it 23-12 and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 299. The act sets rules for companies selling home solar and battery systems. A company has to give the customer written disclosures before a purchase or lease. The customer gets a window to cancel without a penalty, apart from a deposit already agreed as non-refundable. A salesperson cannot knock at a home that has posted a no-soliciting sign, or where a local law bars it. A company cannot use the state's name, logo or images to suggest the state backs it. It also cannot buy sales leads that were gathered in ways the act forbids. The Colorado House passed it 43-22 and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 1217. The act tightens the rules on funeral businesses. Stealing money a client paid for funeral services is now both a deceptive trade practice and a crime. Pre-need funeral contracts do not include transportation protection agreements. The act also moves the date by which someone training as a mortuary practitioner has to have 4,000 hours of work experience. The Colorado House passed it 46-15 and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 1322. Home insurers already have to send a policyholder a certified copy of their policy within 30 days of a request. The act says the request has to be in writing and go to the carrier's registered agent. A carrier that misses the deadline owes $50 for each day the copy is late. The Colorado House passed it 42-20 and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's changes to House Bill 1182 and pass it. Some insurers price home policies using computer models of wildfire and disaster risk. The act makes an insurer using such a model share information about it with state regulators when it files rates. The insurer has to take account of steps a homeowner took to reduce risk. It also has to publish what discounts are available for that work. The Colorado House voted 42-20 to accept those changes and pass the bill, and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 1179. The act makes car insurance pay to replace a child car seat damaged in a crash. When someone files a claim, the insurer has to ask whether a car seat was in the vehicle. If there was one, the policy covering the crash pays to replace it or repays what the owner spent. The Colorado House passed it 40-22 and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to adopt the conference committee's report on House Bill 1300 and pass it. The act changes how an injured worker gets treated under workers' compensation. When a doctor asks to approve care, the employer or insurer has to answer using the state division's treatment standards. The employer or insurer also has to tell the worker in writing, within seven days of hearing about the injury, that the worker can pick the treating doctor. The notice has to say where to find the state's list of accredited doctors. The worker picks from that list, normally within 70 miles of home or work. The limit stretches to 100 miles, or further for good cause, when few accredited doctors nearby will take the case. The Colorado House voted 41-24 to adopt that report and pass the bill, and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 1329. Some companies pay a side's legal costs in a lawsuit in return for part of any award. The act targets those funders that a government of concern owns or controls. Such a funder has to file with the Colorado attorney general when the case starts. The filing has to name the funder and include a copy of the funding agreement. Breaking the rule counts as an unfair or deceptive trade practice. The Colorado House passed it 46-16 and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 52. State law used to keep every railroad accident report made for the utilities commission secret. The act ends that blanket secrecy. The commission can still write rules to protect an open inquiry or security details. Those rules cannot hide a finished report, which has to be released on time. The Colorado Senate passed it 23-12 and the governor signed it into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 72. Kratom is a plant product sold in shops, and Colorado already bars selling it to anyone under 21. The act makes several kratom sales a deceptive trade practice. Those include selling to someone under 21, leaving it where someone under 21 can reach it, and selling lab-made kratom compounds. The state and buyers can act on a breach. The Colorado House passed it 47-18 and the governor signed it into law.
